summary.text: 大 is a whole-graph picture of a standing adult human. It is commonly used to mean “big” and “great”; “adult” is proposed as an earlier sense, though a dated sequence linking the two is lacking.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph depicts a frontal human figure. Descriptions differ on whether the arms hang down or extend outward, so the pose is not settled; the figure’s interpretation does not depend on the popular outstretched-arms explanation.

components.text: The whole graph is analyzed as a frontal standing adult human, not as a combination of smaller signs. Descriptions differ on the arms’ position; the figure and its proposed original sense remain interpretations.

history.text: Historical accounts label forms as oracle-bone, bronze, small-seal and standard script, describing the standard form as close to small seal. The curated oracle-bone, bronze and seal examples are modern redrawings that show broad stylistic differences, not a precise sequence of stroke changes.
An Eastern Han dictionary explanation says 大 depicts a human and records it as an ancient form of 亣. This is an early historical account of the graph, not independent proof of its prehistoric origin.

uncertainties.text: The earliest precisely dated use meaning “adult” or “big” is unresolved. A bronze inscription is cited for “big,” but its specific vessel and date are not established.

The proposed development from “adult” to “big” lacks a dated sequence of intermediate uses. The broad script labels likewise do not establish specific graphic changes, corruption or variant chronology.

senses.text: A specialist analysis proposes “adult,” contrasted with child, as an early sense; a precisely dated attestation for this use is unresolved.

senses.period: bronze inscription reported; exact date unresolved
senses.text: A bronze inscription is cited using 大 for “big,” opposite 小; the specific vessel and date are unresolved.

developments.text: An analysis proposes that “big” developed from “adult,” but intermediate stages are not documented in a dated sequence.
Both senses are recorded, but the evidence does not establish that “great” developed from “big” or provide a chronology linking them.

limitations.text: The proposed adult-to-big development is an interpretation rather than a dated chain of attestations; the earliest precisely dated sense remains unresolved.
Modern glosses do not establish a historical sequence among “big,” “great,” “vast,” “large” and “high.”

items.period: Shang period style; the page identifies the script style, not a securely dated specimen in the SVG itself
items.caption: This oracle-bone-style form shows a frontal human figure with a vertical body, arms extending to either side, and separated legs. It fits the analysis of 大 as a human figure, though the precise pose and original sense remain interpretations.
items.alt: Black oracle-bone-style glyph with a long upright body, outstretched arms, and two separated legs.
items.selection_reason: The candidate gives a useful early-style example for the human-figure analysis. Its visible pose also makes clear why “arms outstretched” is a shape description, not proof of the graph’s original meaning.

items.caption: This Western Zhou bronze-style redraw retains a frontal human-like form, with a tall central body, lateral arms, and legs below. A bronze inscription cited in the specialist account uses 大 opposite 小, but this redraw alone does not establish that usage or a precise date.
items.alt: Black bronze-script-style glyph with a tall central stroke, broad arms, and two curved legs.
items.selection_reason: It adds a visually distinct bronze-script form and connects to the reported bronze use meaning “big”; the inscription evidence is cited separately from the image’s appearance.

items.caption: This Shuowen seal-style redraw has a balanced human-like outline: a central upright stroke, arms slanting outward, and two long legs. It illustrates a dictionary-script form without establishing a stroke-by-stroke path from earlier forms.

limitations.text: These are modern redrawings in named script styles, not photographs of ancient objects. The adult-human interpretation is supported by specialist analysis, but the visible pose does not by itself establish the graph’s original meaning; one local account’s “outstretched arms” explanation conflicts with the analysis of arms hanging down.

The images permit broad comparison of script styles, but they do not establish a precise chronology of graphic changes or the earliest dated use. The adult-to-big semantic development is a proposed analysis, and its intermediate stages are not documented here.
